notes.why: Dim light and bright light (Hess 1923): in near darkness the field leans toward the bright side and in ordinary light it leans away. Easy; the draft's thresholds are invented.

A sudden fall in brightness (a third within a third of a second) closes the field to a point and reopens it over two or three seconds, as a fan worm withdraws (Bok 2017). Needs a brightness trigger the engine lacks.
A mole digging: a low rumble raises and brightens the field, as an earthworm surfaces (Catania 2008). Needs the microphone's low band, with consent.
A leech's body of eyes: with the phone flat and face up, the top half leans green and the bottom half blue (Stowasser 2019). Needs zones and device orientation.
The draft proposes separate millipede and centipede views; until they exist the word table sends them here.

rows: An earthworm has no eyes. Light-sensitive cells lie in the skin of every segment, most of them at the head and the tail, and tiny windows in a layer of pigment let light reach them from set directions.
An earthworm crawls away from ordinary light, but it moves toward light that is very dim.

Florida earthworms rush out of their burrows when the ground carries the vibration of a digging mole. Bait collectors copy it by scraping a stake driven into the soil, and worms come up as far as 12 metres away.

A medicinal leech has five pairs of eyecups on its head and seven pairs of light-sensing spots in every segment of its body. The spots on its back respond best to green light, and those underneath to ultraviolet.

Each cup-shaped eye of a freshwater planarian samples the world about every 35 degrees, and behaviour tests on another planarian give the same coarse sharpness. Planarians flee ultraviolet light most strongly, and worms without eyes, or without heads, still flee near-ultraviolet light. Land planarians, such as the hammerhead worms, have many tiny eyes on the head.

Fan worms and Christmas tree worms have eyes on their feathery tentacles. Their light-sensing pigment peaks at 464 nanometres, close to the blue light of a shallow reef, and a passing shadow makes them pull back into their tubes at once.

Worms meet most of the world through touch, taste and moisture. A leech's skin answers vibration up to about 50 times a second, and land planarians need damp ground to live. None of this reaches a camera.

This view shows only how much light there is, where it comes from and how it changes. It weights blue light most, because planarians and the underside of a leech answer ultraviolet most strongly and blue is the nearest colour the camera records. The weighting is the app's own choice.
